questions.q: what do we learn about the queen’s condition?
points: she has been wounded for a long time (iamdudum saucia)
by a deep anxiety / love (gravi … cura)
she feeds the wound (vulnus alit)
in her veins (venis)
she is consumed by a hidden fire (caeco carpitur igni)

questions.q: what keeps coming back to Dido’s mind, and what effect does this have on her?
points: again and again (multa … multusque recursat)
his courage (viri virtus)
the honour of his family / line (gentis honos)
his face / looks (vultus) and his words (verbaque)
stay fixed in her heart (haerent infixi pectore)
her love / anxiety lets her body have no peaceful rest (nec placidam membris dat cura quietem)

questions.q: explain in your own words what Dido’s love is doing to her.
points: she cannot stop thinking of his face and his words (haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque)
she cannot sleep / get any peaceful rest (nec placidam … dat cura quietem)
her body gets no relief (membris)

questions.q: what time is it, and how does Virgil describe it?
points: it is the next day (postera)
the sun was lighting the earth with his lamp (Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras)
dawn had cleared the dewy shadow from the sky (umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram)

questions.q: what do we learn here about Dido and Anna?
points: Dido is hardly in her right mind (male sana)
she speaks to her sister (adloquitur … sororem)
her sister shares her every thought (unanimam)

questions.q: what does Dido tell Anna about her night?
points: dreams (insomnia)
terrify her (terrent)
and leave her uneasy / in suspense (me suspensam)

questions.q: who is this guest, and how had he come to Carthage?
points: Aeneas
he had been shipwrecked on Dido’s coast (and she had taken in the Trojans)

questions.q: what does Dido say about the newcomer?
points: he is new (novus)
he has come into their home (nostris successit sedibus)
as a guest (hospes)
he has a noble bearing / looks (quem sese ore ferens)
a brave heart (forti pectore)
and is strong in arms (armis)

questions.q: explain why Dido believes that Aeneas comes from the gods.
points: she really believes it (credo equidem)
and says her belief is not idle (nec vana fides)
that his family is divine (genus esse deorum)
because fear shows a low-born spirit (degeneres animos timor arguit), and he showed none

questions.q: what moves Dido about Aeneas’ story?
points: the fates by which he has been tossed about (quibus ille iactatus fatis)
the wars he told of (quae bella … canebat)
which he endured to the end (exhausta)

questions.q: describe Dido’s state at the start of Book 4.
points: she has long been wounded (iamdudum saucia)
she feeds the wound in her veins (vulnus alit venis)
she is consumed by a hidden fire (caeco carpitur igni)
Aeneas’ courage keeps returning to her mind (multa viri virtus animo … recursat)
and the honour of his family (gentis honos)
his face and words are fixed in her heart (haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque)
she gets no peaceful rest (nec placidam membris dat cura quietem)

questions.q: when, and to whom, did Dido speak, and in what state was she?
points: the next day / at dawn (postera)
to her sister (sororem)
who shared her every thought (unanimam)
she was hardly in her right mind (male sana)

questions.q: what has Dido decided, and why?
points: it is fixed and immovable in her mind (animo fixum immotumque sederet)
that she would not join herself to anyone (ne cui me … vellem sociare)
in marriage (vinclo … iugali)
since her first love deceived her (primus amor deceptam … fefellit)
by his death (morte)
she has come to hate marriage (pertaesum thalami taedaeque)

questions.lemma: huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae
questions.q: what does Dido admit here?
points: perhaps (forsan)
she could have given way (potui succumbere)
to this one fault (huic uni … culpae)

questions.q: why does Dido say she will not marry again?
points: her first love (primus amor)
deceived / cheated her (deceptam … fefellit)
by his death (morte)

questions.q: what does Dido confess to Anna?
points: she will admit it (fatebor enim)
since the death (post fata) of her poor husband Sychaeus (miseri … Sychaei coniugis)
and since her household gods were spattered with blood (sparsos … penates)
when her brother murdered him (fraterna caede)
this man alone (solus hic)
has moved her feelings (inflexit sensus)
and stirred her wavering heart (animumque labantem impulit)

questions.q: who was Sychaeus, and how had he died?
points: Dido’s first husband
he was murdered by her brother (Pygmalion, king of Tyre)
for his wealth

questions.q: explain what Dido recognises.
points: she recognises (agnosco)
the signs (vestigia)
of the old flame, the love she once felt for Sychaeus (veteris … flammae)

questions.q: what would Dido rather suffer than break her vow?
points: that the earth should gape open (tellus … dehiscat)
to its depths (ima)
or that the almighty father (pater omnipotens)
should drive her down with his thunderbolt (adigat me fulmine)
to the pale shadows of Erebus (pallentes umbras Erebi)
and deep night (noctemque profundam)
before she wrongs Honour (ante pudor quam te violo)
or breaks its laws (tua iura resolvo)

questions.q: who is meant?
points: Jupiter

questions.q: what does Dido say about her first husband?
points: he first joined her to himself (primus qui me sibi iunxit)
he has taken her love away with him (meos … amores abstulit)
let him keep it (habeat secum)
and guard it in his grave (servetque sepulcro)

questions.q: how does Dido’s speech end?
points: she finishes speaking (sic effata)
she fills her lap (sinum … implevit)
with welling tears (lacrimis … obortis)

questions.q: what does Dido reveal about her past and her present feelings?
points: her mind is fixed against remarrying (animo fixum immotumque)
her first love cheated her by his death (primus amor deceptam morte fefellit)
she has come to hate marriage (pertaesum thalami taedaeque)
perhaps she could give way (forsan potui succumbere)
her husband was murdered by her brother (fraterna caede)
this man alone has moved her feelings (solus hic inflexit sensus)
her heart was already wavering (animumque labantem)

questions.q: explain in your own words how Dido declares her loyalty to Sychaeus.
points: she would rather be swallowed by the earth (tellus … dehiscat)
or struck down by Jupiter’s thunderbolt (fulmine)
than break her vow of honour (quam te violo)
her love belongs to her first husband (meos … amores abstulit)
and he should keep it in his grave (servetque sepulcro)

questions.q: how does Anna address Dido?
points: as dearer to her sister than the light itself (luce magis dilecta sorori)
with deep affection (o … dilecta)

questions.q: what does Anna say Dido will miss if she stays alone?
points: she will be worn away (carpere)
alone and grieving (solane … maerens)
all through her youth (perpetua … iuventa)
she will never know sweet children (nec dulces natos)
or the rewards of love (Veneris … praemia)

questions.q: what does Anna suggest about the dead?
points: she asks whether Dido really believes (credis)
that ashes or the spirits in their graves (cinerem aut manes … sepultos)
care about such things (id … curare)

questions.q: how does Anna argue that this love is different from Dido’s past refusals?
points: she grants the point (esto)
no suitors moved Dido in her grief (aegram nulli … flexere mariti)
not in Libya, not before that in Tyre (non Libyae, non ante Tyro)
she rejected Iarbas (despectus Iarbas)
and the other chieftains (ductoresque alii) of Africa (Africa terra)
but now she would be fighting (pugnabis)
against a love that pleases her (placitone … amori)

questions.q: who was Iarbas?
points: a North African king who had wanted to marry Dido (and who sold her the land for Carthage)

questions.q: what does Anna ask Dido to remember?
points: whose lands she has settled in (quorum consederis arvis)
it has not occurred to her (nec venit in mentem)

questions.q: what dangers does Anna say surround Carthage?
points: the cities of the Gaetulians (Gaetulae urbes)
a people unconquerable in war (genus insuperabile bello)
the unbridled Numidians (Numidae infreni)
the inhospitable Syrtis (inhospita Syrtis)
a region deserted because of drought (deserta siti regio)
the Barcaeans, raging far and wide (lateque furentes Barcaei)
war rising from Tyre (bella Tyro surgentia)
the threats of her brother (germanique minas)

questions.q: describe the neighbours that Anna lists.
points: the Gaetulians, unconquerable in war (genus insuperabile bello)
the Numidians, without bridles / wild (Numidae infreni)
the Syrtis, which is inhospitable (inhospita Syrtis)
a region made desert by drought (deserta siti regio)
the Barcaeans, raging far and wide (lateque furentes Barcaei)
they hem Carthage in on both sides (hinc … hinc)

questions.q: what further dangers does Anna mention?
points: war rising from Tyre (bella Tyro surgentia)
the threats of Dido’s brother (germanique minas)
she says she need not even mention them (quid … dicam)

questions.q: who is Dido’s brother?
points: Pygmalion, king of Tyre (who murdered Sychaeus)

questions.q: what arguments does Anna use in her opening lines?
points: Dido is dearer to her than the light (luce magis dilecta)
Dido will grieve alone (solane … maerens)
all through her youth (perpetua … iuventa)
she will have no sweet children (nec dulces natos)
and none of the rewards of love (Veneris … praemia)
the dead do not care (id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos)

questions.q: what does Anna believe about the Trojans’ arrival?
points: she believes (reor) it happened with the gods as protectors (dis … auspicibus)
and with Juno’s favour (Iunone secunda)
the Trojan ships (Iliacas … carinas)
held this course with the wind (hunc cursum … vento tenuisse)

questions.q: whose goddess was Juno, and what was her attitude to the Trojans?
points: she was the patron goddess of Carthage
she was the enemy of the Trojans / of Aeneas

questions.q: what future does Anna predict for Carthage?
points: Dido will see a great city (quam tu urbem … cernes)
a kingdom will rise (quae surgere regna)
from such a marriage (coniugio tali)
with the Trojans’ arms alongside (Teucrum comitantibus armis)
Carthage’s glory will rise to great heights (Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus)

questions.q: what does Anna tell Dido to do, and why will it work?
points: ask the gods for their goodwill (posce deos veniam)
once the sacrifices are favourably received (sacrisque litatis)
give herself over to hospitality (indulge hospitio)
weave reasons for delay (causasque innecte morandi)
while winter rages on the sea (dum pelago desaevit hiems)
and rainy Orion (aquosus Orion)
the ships are battered (quassataeque rates)
and the sky is unmanageable (non tractabile caelum)

questions.q: what does Anna advise Dido to do?
points: ask the gods for their goodwill (posce deos veniam)
after favourable sacrifices (sacrisque litatis)
give herself over to hospitality (indulge hospitio)
weave reasons for delay (causasque innecte morandi)

questions.q: explain why Anna thinks Aeneas will have to stay.
points: winter is raging on the sea (dum pelago desaevit hiems)
rainy Orion brings storms (aquosus Orion)
his ships are battered (quassataeque rates)
the sky is unmanageable (non tractabile caelum)

questions.q: what is Orion here?
points: a constellation, whose setting in early winter was linked with storms at sea

questions.q: what effect do Anna’s words have on Dido?
points: they set her heart ablaze (animum flammavit)
with a boundless passion (impenso … amore)
they gave hope (spemque dedit) to her wavering mind (dubiae menti)
they broke down her sense of honour (solvitque pudorem)

questions.q: explain in your own words what happened to Dido’s mind.
points: she was given hope (spemque dedit)
where her mind had been wavering (dubiae menti)
her sense of honour was broken down (solvitque pudorem)

questions.q: how does Anna argue that a marriage with Aeneas would benefit Carthage?
points: the gods protected the Trojans’ voyage (dis … auspicibus)
Juno favoured it (Iunone secunda)
the Trojan ships were guided here (hunc cursum … tenuisse)
Dido will see a great city (quam tu urbem)
a kingdom will rise (quae surgere regna)
from such a marriage (coniugio tali)
Trojan arms will march beside theirs (Teucrum comitantibus armis)
Carthage’s glory will rise (Punica … gloria)

essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido’s love as a sickness and a torment?
points: Dido has already been suffering for a long time when the book opens
her love is a wound that she keeps feeding instead of letting it heal
it is a hidden fire that eats her away from inside
Aeneas’ courage and family keep returning to her thoughts
his face and words are fixed in her heart, and she cannot sleep
a calm, bright dawn comes while she has had no rest
she is hardly in her right mind when she speaks to Anna
her first words are about dreams that terrify her

essays.q: how does Virgil show that Dido is dazzled by Aeneas?
points: Dido speaks to her sister at dawn, hardly in her right mind
she has been kept awake and terrified by dreams
she bursts out with questions about the new guest in her home
she admires his bearing, his courage and his strength in arms
she is sure that he is descended from the gods
she argues that his lack of fear proves his noble birth
she pities him for the fates that have tossed him about
she is moved by the wars he has told of

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a vivid opening to Book 4?
points: the book opens with the queen already wounded by love
her love is pictured as a wound and a hidden fire
Aeneas’ qualities, face and words fill her thoughts
she spends a sleepless night while a calm dawn rises
she turns to her sister, who shares her every thought
she pours out her feelings in a rush of exclamations and questions
she praises Aeneas as divine, brave and noble
she pities him for his sufferings and the wars he has endured

essays.q: how does Virgil show the conflict in Dido’s mind?
points: Dido insists that her decision not to remarry is fixed and immovable
she explains that her first love cheated her by dying
she says that she has come to hate marriage
yet she admits that she could perhaps have given way to this one fault
she confesses to Anna that Aeneas alone has moved her
she recalls the murder of Sychaeus by her brother
her heart is described as already wavering
she recognises the signs of the love she once felt

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s oath of loyalty to Sychaeus powerful?
points: Dido confesses that Aeneas alone has moved her since Sychaeus’ death
she recalls the bloody murder of her husband by her brother
she recognises the old flame of love returning
she would rather the earth swallowed her
or that Jupiter struck her down to the underworld with his thunderbolt
she addresses Honour directly and swears not to break its laws
she insists that her love belongs to Sychaeus in his grave
her speech ends with her lap full of tears

essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido’s struggle between her new love and her loyalty to Sychaeus?
points: she claims her resolve not to remarry is fixed
her first love was taken from her by death
she admits she might have given way to this one fault
she confesses that Aeneas alone has stirred her wavering heart
she recognises the signs of her old love
she swears she would rather die than break her vow
she declares that Sychaeus keeps her love in his grave
she ends in tears, which shows how weak her defences are

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s arguments persuasive?
points: Anna begins with deep affection for her sister
she asks whether Dido will waste her youth in lonely grief
she reminds her of the children and love she would miss
she dismisses the idea that the dead care
she concedes Dido’s past refusals of suitors such as Iarbas
she asks whether Dido will fight a love that pleases her
she lists the hostile peoples surrounding Carthage
she ends with the threat of war from Tyre and from Dido’s brother

essays.q: how does Virgil present Anna’s appeal to Dido’s feelings?
points: Anna calls Dido dearer to her than the light
she pictures Dido worn away by lonely grief
she stresses that Dido is still young
she offers the prospect of sweet children and love
she suggests that the dead do not care
she grants that Dido has refused other suitors
she argues that resisting a welcome love is a pointless fight
she turns to remind Dido of the land she has settled in

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s political argument for the marriage convincing?
points: Anna reminds Dido whose lands she has settled in
she lists warlike and wild peoples on every side
even the land and the coast are hostile
she hints at war from Tyre and Dido’s brother
she claims the gods and Juno guided the Trojan ships
she imagines the great city and kingdom that would rise
Trojan arms would march beside Carthage’s
Carthage’s glory would be raised to great heights

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s vision of the future persuasive?
points: Anna believes the gods and Juno brought the Trojans to Carthage
she imagines the great city and kingdom that would rise
she already calls the match a marriage
Trojan arms would support Carthage and raise its glory
she makes the next steps sound easy: prayers and hospitality
she suggests weaving reasons to delay Aeneas
the winter storms will keep the Trojan ships in port
her words set Dido’s heart ablaze and break down her honour

essays.q: how does Virgil show Anna’s words overcoming Dido’s resistance?
points: Anna paints a glorious picture of the city Dido will see
she speaks of the match as a marriage
she promises Trojan support and Carthaginian glory
she tells Dido she need only ask the gods for goodwill
she presents love as the duty of hospitality
she advises weaving reasons for delay
the winter weather makes delay seem sensible
Dido is set ablaze, given hope, and loses her sense of honour

essays.q: how does Virgil present Anna as a skilful persuader?
points: she claims the support of the gods and of Juno
she makes the Trojans’ arrival seem divinely guided
she excites Dido with a vision of a great city and kingdom
she names the match a marriage
she presents Aeneas as a powerful ally for Carthage
she makes the next steps sound simple
she dresses up love as hospitality
she gives practical reasons why Aeneas must stay through the winter
